text: Apple is your enemy, and if you don't recognize this and fight, you're being a chump.
If the users don't control the program, the program controls the users.
Facebook is not your friend, it is a surveillance engine.
You must consider every proprietary program as potential malware.
Cloud computing is a trap designed to force people into careless computing.
Digital Restrictions Management is a mechanism for turning computers into jails.
With software, there are only two possibilities: freedom or subjugation.
Proprietary software is an injustice because it denies users freedom.
Steve Jobs, the pioneer of the computer as a jail made cool, designed to sever fools from their freedom, has died. I'm not glad he's dead, but I'm glad he's gone.
Apple pioneered making products into digital handcuffs, designed specifically to lock users into a cage and block them from controlling their own computing.
Proprietary software tends to have malicious features. When users don't have the source code, we can never tell what spyware or back doors corporations put in.
Amazon's Kindle is an electronic swindle designed to attack traditional readers' rights: to acquire books anonymously, to share them, and to keep them forever.
Everyone who uses the term 'intellectual property' is either confused himself or trying to confuse you by lumping disparate laws together for corporate profit.
Non-free software is not just an inconvenience; it is a social problem. It is a system of unjust corporate power over users.
The iPad is not a computer for empowering human beings. It is an iBad designed as an authoritarian prison where Apple decides what you can read and run.
Windows is proprietary malware. Microsoft designs operating systems that snoop on users, report their activities, and force unsolicited changes upon them.
One reason you should not use web applications to do your computing is that you lose control. It is just as bad as using a proprietary program.
The goal of free software is not merely to write code; it is to establish a free society where users cooperate and control their own technology.

Steve Jobs made computing shiny and fashionable, but his true legacy was transforming the general-purpose computer into an appliance prison. He proved that millions of people would cheerfully pay to be locked up, as long as the prison walls were sleek and brushed aluminum. We must reject the computer as a digital jail.

When Amazon remotely erased copies of George Orwell's 1984 from users' Kindles, they demonstrated the ultimate danger of corporate control. A company can reach into your hands and confiscate your books because they own the software and the platform. That is not progress; that is technological totalitarianism.

Using a proprietary program means putting yourself at the mercy of the corporation that owns it. They can put in spyware to monitor you, back doors to attack you, and digital restrictions management to stop you from sharing with your neighbor. The only defense against corporate tyranny in computing is software freedom.

Software as a Service is another corporate trap. When you do your computing on somebody else's server with proprietary web applications, you surrender control of your data and your freedom completely. It is careless computing disguised as convenience.

Corporations tell you that without restrictive copyright and digital locks, creativity will vanish. In reality, their digital handcuffs are designed to strangle cultural participation and ensure that access to knowledge remains a gated toll road that only they control.

If you look at the history of computing, corporations have constantly attempted to dispossess users of the right to modify and inspect their machines. They treat general-purpose computing as a threat to their recurring revenues. Freedom is the only safeguard against this digital serfdom.

Proprietary software corporations have built a business model based on dividing users and conquering them. First, they prohibit users from sharing software with their friends, destroying social solidarity. Second, they withhold the source code so users cannot understand or modify what the program actually does. Third, they introduce backdoors, spyware, and digital restrictions to enforce corporate monopolies. Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, and Google have turned personal computing into an instrument of corporate surveillance. To reclaim our autonomy, we must reject their digital handcuffs and insist on free software.

The true enemy of user freedom is the seductive comfort of corporate paternalism. Companies like Apple tell their customers, 'Trust us, we will take care of everything, you do not need to look under the hood.' But in exchanging freedom for convenience, users surrender their digital autonomy and accept censorship. When a single boardroom in Cupertino decides what applications you are permitted to run on your own pocket device, computing has ceased to be an emancipatory tool and has become an instrument of authoritarian control. Every restriction, every DRM layer, and every closed application repository is an explicit statement that the user is not the rightful master of the machine they purchased.
To say that you 'own' a file is a linguistic trick designed to confuse you. What you own is a paper record; the file itself belongs to the corporation that issued it.

If you want to share, don't use the internet. Use USB sticks. Give your friend the file directly. That's the only way to be sure they actually have the software, rather than a souped-up tracking device.

Steve Jobs was a pioneer of digital control. He transformed personal computing into a system of restrictions, convincing millions that being locked down was a feature. But freedom is not a bug to be patched; it is the fundamental requirement for being human.

When you buy a Kindle, you do not buy a book. You purchase a license to read a file that Amazon owns and can delete from your device whenever they please. This is not retail; it is technological servitude.

Every time you use a proprietary program, you are trusting a corporation with your personal data and your freedom. Since you cannot see the source code, you have no way of knowing if they are spying on you, tracking your keystrokes, or locking you into their ecosystem.
We must reject the idea that convenience is more important than freedom. Convenience is a temptation; freedom is a right. You cannot build a just society on a foundation of technological servitude.
The Free Software movement is not merely about writing code; it is about organizing communities and changing social dynamics. When we share, we build solidarity; when we restrict, we isolate.
Amazon's business model relies on turning books into temporary licenses. They want you to be a reader, not a possessor. But reading is a personal act, not a subscription service.
Proprietary software is designed to enforce obedience. The user becomes a subject, not a citizen, of the digital realm. Only free software restores the citizen's power to question and modify.
We are not antisocial just because we refuse to use software that violates our freedom. We are defending the rights of the entire computing community, not just ourselves.
The goal of the Free Software Foundation is not to make users dependent on free software; it is to empower users to be free from dependency on any software.

Using a proprietary system is like living in a prison where the warden tells you what books you can read, what food you can eat, and when you can leave your cell. We must demand the keys to our own digital lives.
When we speak of 'intellectual property,' we are speaking of a corporate weapon designed to suppress independent creativity and ensure that only those who pay tribute may participate in culture.
The 'cloud' is a euphemism for corporate servers where your data is processed, analyzed, and controlled without your knowledge. It is not a service; it is a surrender of privacy.

Corporations have convinced the public that proprietary software is necessary for security. In reality, closed code is a security risk because it prevents users from identifying and fixing vulnerabilities. Free software is inherently more secure because it is transparent.
Apple's iPhone is a Trojan horse. It looks like a personal computer, but inside it is a prison designed to monitor and control your every action. We must reject these digital handcuffs.
Using an app store is surrendering your autonomy. You are asking a corporation for permission to run software on your own device. Freedom is not given; it is taken.
The free software movement is a movement for social justice. When we deny people the right to use and share software, we are denying them the right to participate fully in society.
Copyright is not about protecting artists; it is about protecting corporations. It is a legal construct designed to turn creativity into a source of profit through exclusion.

A library is a place where you can check out a book, read it, take notes, and share your thoughts with others. That is how knowledge should function. Proprietary software seeks to turn libraries into prisons.
When a company develops a new technology, their first instinct is not to make life better for users, but to find ways to control users and extract more value from them.
The Free Software Movement asks only for the freedom to use, study, modify, and share software. There is nothing radical about that; it is the foundation of all meaningful progress.
To be truly free, one must control the tools they use. In the 21st century, that means controlling our software. If we do not have that control, we are not free.
Digital Restrictions Management (DRM) is not about convenience; it is about coercion. It is a system designed to make you a prisoner of the products you purchase.
We should not be grateful to corporations for giving us software; we should be demanding that they respect our rights as users and citizens.
The distinction between 'free' as in 'gratis' and 'free' as in 'libre' is crucial. We are fighting for the freedom to use, not the freedom to pay less.
When we accept software that restricts our freedom, we are accepting a form of digital servitude. There is no middle ground: either we control our computing, or it controls us.
The corporate argument is simple: if you give users freedom, they will make a mess. But a messy freedom is infinitely preferable to a clean prison.
Proprietary software developers are not creating tools; they are creating chains. Each line of closed code is another link in a chain that binds the user to the corporation.
We must stop thanking companies for 'listening to our feedback.' We should be demanding that they respect our rights. Gratitude for crumbs does not feed the hungry.
The internet was once a tool for sharing and collaboration. Now, for most users, it is a system of surveillance and control. We must reclaim it for freedom.
A computer that cannot be modified by its user is not a personal computer; it is a restricted appliance. We should not be fooled by marketing language.
When we talk about 'intellectual property,' we are talking about a system that prioritizes profit over people. It is a legal framework designed to restrict access to knowledge and culture.
Software as a Service is a return to the mainframe era, but with a corporate twist. You do not own your data, you do not own your tools, and you do not own your work. You are merely renting access.
The fight for free software is a fight for democracy in the digital age. If citizens cannot control the technology they use, they cannot be truly free citizens.
We should not be afraid to be called antisocial for refusing to use spyware. Sometimes, protecting our principles requires us to stand apart from the crowd.
If we do not stand up for software freedom now, we will find ourselves in a future where all our computing is done on machines we do not control, by corporations we do not trust.
The purpose of the Free Software Foundation is to ensure that the cooperative spirit of computing survives and thrives, even in the face of corporate attempts to monopolize it.
Every time you choose free software, you are making a political statement. You are saying that freedom, cooperation, and user control matter more than corporate profits.
The idea that we must surrender our freedom for security is a false dichotomy. True security comes from transparency and community, not from hidden backdoors and corporate control.
We are not against innovation; we are against the idea that innovation must come at the cost of human freedom. Technological progress should empower people, not imprison them.
When a company tells you that a feature is 'for your convenience,' ask yourself: whose convenience? Often, what is convenient for the user is inconvenient for the corporation.
Digital Restrictions Management is not a solution to piracy; it is a tool for oppression. It treats all users as potential criminals and restricts them accordingly.
The free software movement is a practical movement for real change. We do not just talk about freedom; we build systems that embody it.
If we want a future where technology serves humanity, we must actively build that future. We cannot wait for corporations to grant us permission.

LinkedIn recently deleted lots of fake accounts that pretended to have been employed by prestigious companies. Some fake accounts claim to have been the head of digital security for various companies. Those may be aimed at getting people to accept malicious security advice.
LinkedIn requires you to use non-free Javascript to access the site.
